item.title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Leadership: Processes, Practices, and Contexts
item.content:encoded:
Bruno Fischer, University of Campinas

Aki Harima, Tallinn University of Technology

Sophia Behr, University of Stuttgart

Philip T. Roundy, University of Tennessee Chattanooga

Erik Stam, Utrecht University

Maribel Guerrero, Arizona State University

This special issue examines leadership within entrepreneurial ecosystems as a central yet underexplored phenomenon shaping ecosystem dynamics and outcomes. Rather than treating leadership as a residual category of individual actors or positions, the issue conceptualizes it as a relational process through which direction develops, priorities are negotiated, support is mobilized, and ecosystem development is influenced. The focus spans stable, transforming, and crisis-affected ecosystems, recognizing that contexts such as digitalization, sustainability transitions, and geopolitical disruptions shape how leadership emerges and evolves.

The special issue seeks to move beyond describing static ecosystem structures toward explaining how collective action is generated, coordinated, and sustained over time. It welcomes diverse theoretical perspectives and methodological approaches that develop, challenge, extend, or offer alternative conceptualizations of EE leadership. Research should address who assumes leadership roles, how legitimacy and followership emerge, and how different leadership configurations can compensate for weaknesses in networks, resources, or institutions.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualization and theory of entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) leadership across formal, informal, individual, collective, organizational, distributed, relational, and processual perspectives
  • Dimensions and manifestations of EE leadership (e.g., public, entrepreneurial, community)
  • Interaction between EE leadership and other ecosystem elements such as networks, institutions, finance, or culture
  • Contextual uniqueness shaping forms and theorization of EE leadership across different institutional, cultural, and geographical settings
  • Elements of EE leadership affecting how entrepreneurs and supportive agents cohere around shared norms, values, and goals
  • Relational characteristics (e.g., coordination, collaboration, communication) supporting effective ecosystem leadership
  • Participation, legitimacy, and authority emergence in EE leadership processes
  • How characteristics of ecosystem actors (lived experience, place attachment, prosocial orientation, identity) shape participation in ecosystem leadership
  • Activities, practices, and processes constituting ecosystem leadership and their collective goals
  • Distribution of leadership activities across ecosystem actors and how interactions shape collective direction and coordinated action
  • Forms of leadership and agency emergence, evolution, and enabling coordinated action within EEs
  • Evolution of ecosystem leadership across phases of development and consequences of different forms
  • Conditions under which leadership can compensate for weaknesses in other ecosystem elements
  • Differences in EE leadership across unstable, transforming, and crisis-affected contexts
  • Direction provision under sustainability pressures, digital transformation, geopolitical tension, or resource disruption
  • Negotiation of competing priorities through EE leadership during simultaneous disruptions
  • Measurement and integration of EE leadership activities, practices, and relational processes into existing ecosystem measurement frameworks
  • Use of network metrics to assess distribution of participation, influence, and coordination within EE leadership processes
  • Measures capturing whether EE leadership is concentrated or distributed, formal or informal, and how these configurations change over time

Timeline

  • December 14, 2026: Online information and early-ideas session for scholars interested in contributing to the special issue
  • February 11, 2027: Paper development workshop within the conference Entrepreneurial Ecosystems in Times of Rapid Transformation in Tallinn, Estonia
  • December 31, 2027: Manuscript submission deadline

item.title: Deciphering Indigenous Entrepreneurship: A Global Driver of Sustainable Regional Development
item.content:encoded:
Meena Chavan, Macquarie University

Christina Theodoraki, IAE Aix-Marseille University

Michelle Evans, University of Melbourne

Jane Menzies, University of Sunshine Coast

Anna Earl, University of Canterbury

Alex Maritz, La Trobe University

Bella Galperin, University of Tampa

This special issue examines Indigenous-led enterprises as drivers of sustainable regional development. Indigenous entrepreneurs worldwide create ventures that blend economic ambition with cultural stewardship, community well-being, and sustainability, often emerging from contexts of historical marginalization and systemic exclusion. The issue broadens geographic scope beyond Anglophone regions to include insights from Latin America, Asia, Africa, and beyond, recognizing Indigenous entrepreneurship as a global phenomenon.

The special issue situates Indigenous entrepreneurship at the intersection of place-based enterprise, sustainability, and regional development. Indigenous ventures are deeply embedded in specific lands, ecosystems, and social networks, operating as collective processes that integrate cultural values with business strategy. Many pursue triple bottom-line objectives combining economic, social, and environmental goals, challenging mainstream entrepreneurship paradigms to adopt more inclusive, community-centric frameworks.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Indigenous entrepreneurial ecosystems and community-driven support systems
  • Indigenous enterprise in CSR/ESG and sustainability goals
  • Leadership styles and communal decision processes in Indigenous enterprises
  • Market expansion and authenticity for Indigenous businesses
  • Branding and storytelling around Indigenous cultural heritage
  • Cultural appropriation and intellectual property rights protection
  • Indigenous worldviews integrated into business and management frameworks
  • Entrepreneurship education and capacity-building programs
  • Enterprise as self-determination and pathways to economic independence
  • Technology adoption by Indigenous entrepreneurs
  • Challenges and resilience in Indigenous business development
  • Indigenous women entrepreneurs and their contributions
  • Policy and place-based development initiatives
  • Global comparative perspectives on Indigenous entrepreneurship
  • Culture-based enterprise models for heritage preservation
  • How Indigenous cultural values shape entrepreneurial decision-making
  • Institutional voids and barriers faced by Indigenous entrepreneurs
  • Community networks, kinship ties, and competitive advantage
  • Balancing profit motives with social and environmental responsibilities

item.title: From Shallow Waters to Deep Dives: Indigenous Theorizing on Chinese Family Enterprises
item.content:encoded:
Bingbing Ge, Lancaster University Management School

Hanqing Fang, Missouri University of Science and Technology

Alfredo De Massis, D'Annunzio University of Chieti-Pescara

Junsheng Dou, Zhejiang University

Winnie Qian Peng, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Indigenous Theorizing and Concept Development: Building indigenous theories rooted in Chinese cultural, institutional, and geopolitical conditions, drawing from Confucian ethics, guanxi logics, or dynastic continuity as explanatory mechanisms
  • Entrepreneurship as Constraint and Renewal: Exploring how institutional and cultural elements such as filial obligation, demographic legacies, and social perceptions shape entrepreneurial succession
  • History-informed research: Taking a history-informed perspective to understand entrepreneurship and family business practices, including innovation through tradition
  • Regional Heterogeneity: Incorporating regional institutional heterogeneity as a central explanatory factor in family entrepreneurship across China's varied development models and cultural norms
  • Purpose in Chinese Business Families: Theorizing Chinese family offices and their approaches to transgenerational wealth through multi-enterprise portfolios and informal arrangements
  • Gender and Patriarchal Paradoxes: Theorizing gendered pathways of leadership specific to the Chinese context and female successors' roles in patriarchal traditions
  • Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG), Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Communal Orientation: Understanding how cultural embeddedness shapes responsibility, CSR, and legitimacy in Chinese family firms
  • Geopolitical Turbulence as Institutional Hybridity: Theorizing how family firms navigate global turbulence under conditions of institutional hybridity and restricted learning opportunities

Timeline

  • February 1, 2026: Extended abstract submission deadline for workshop participation
  • March 1, 2026: Workshop acceptance notification
  • April 11, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • April 11, 2026: ERD Special Issue Workshop at Zhejiang University, China
  • September 1, 2026: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Parenthood and Entrepreneurship: A New Research Agenda
item.content:encoded:
Shuang Lu Frost, Aarhus University

Magdalena Markowska, King's College London

Kai Roland Green, Aarhus University

Kimberly Eddleston, Northeastern University

Alisa Jno-Charles, Babson College

Haibo Zhou, University of Nottingham Ningbo China

Ulla Hytti, University of Turku

Nearly half of early-stage entrepreneurs globally are raising children, yet the intersection of parenthood and entrepreneurship remains underexplored in research. Parent-entrepreneurs face unique tensions between childcare demands and business pressures at individual, family, and societal levels, while entrepreneurship often intensifies rather than resolves work-family conflict. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing effective support systems and policy frameworks that recognize the dual roles many founders navigate.

The special issue seeks both explanatory and interpretive research examining how parenthood shapes and is shaped by entrepreneurial activity across diverse family forms, parental roles, and regional contexts. Key areas include motherhood and entrepreneurship (beyond work-family balance), underexplored topics such as fatherhood, single parenthood, and LGBTQ+ parenting, household dynamics between partners and across generations, and how institutional frameworks and welfare policies influence parent-entrepreneurs differently across regions.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship & Regional Development. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do parent-entrepreneurs negotiate entrepreneurial and parental identities across gender, culture, and sexuality?
  • How do emerging models of fatherhood/motherhood shape entrepreneurship?
  • What role does founder identity transformation play in the transition to entrepreneurial parenthood?
  • How do single parents, LGBTQ+ parents, and individuals in non-normative family forms experience entrepreneurial entry and growth?
  • How is role conflict or role enrichment experienced differently by mothers and fathers in entrepreneurial families?
  • How do partner dynamics and household egalitarianism shape entrepreneurial decisions?
  • What specific resources (cognitive, financial, human, social capital) are transmitted from entrepreneurial parents to children?
  • What are the lived experiences and well-being outcomes of children growing up in entrepreneurial households?
  • How do macro-level factors (e.g., economic instability, policy frameworks) interact with household dynamics to influence children's outcomes and orientations?
  • In what ways do interparental interactions and household role negotiations shape children's perception of entrepreneurship?
  • How do entrepreneurial households balance opportunity creation with potential stress or instability for children?
  • How do regional policies, parental leave systems, and childcare infrastructure shape entrepreneurial entry, continuation, and exit among parents?
  • How do parent-entrepreneurs' experiences differ across welfare regimes (liberal, social-democratic, conservative, developing-country contexts)?
  • What role do informal institutions and extended family networks play in enabling or constraining parental entrepreneurship?
  • How does the portrayal of parent-entrepreneurs in media, public discourse, and cultural narratives affect entrepreneurial motives and sources of satisfaction?
  • How does the self-representation and identity work of parent-entrepreneurs on social media and in entrepreneurial communities contribute to their business success and well-being?
  • How do discursive ideals of 'good motherhood' or 'involved fatherhood' constrain or enable entrepreneurial action?
  • What are the longitudinal effects of entrepreneurship on family well-being, and vice versa?
  • How does parenthood influence innovation, creativity, or business performance?
  • How do entrepreneurial career trajectories differ based on family status, parenting roles, and the timing of parenthood relative to venture creation?

Timeline

  • June 1, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • May 15, 2027: Submission window opens
  • July 1, 2027: Manuscript deadline
